title: Redundancy & Failover Patterns
summary: Infra-level high-availability design — multi-AZ/region topology, failover automation, and graceful degradation when something's still down.

slides.markdown:
**Redundancy** means running more capacity than you need so a failure doesn't become an outage; **failover** is how traffic actually moves off the failed piece.

- Active-active and active-passive are the two core redundancy shapes, with different cost and complexity trade-offs.
- **RTO** (how long to recover) and **RPO** (how much data you can lose) are the numbers that decide which DR tier you need.
- Failing over isn't binary — **graceful degradation** buys time when a full recovery isn't instant.

| | Active-active | Active-passive |
|---|---|---|
| Traffic during normal ops | Split across all instances | Only the active instance serves traffic |
| Cost | Higher — standby capacity does real work | Lower — standby often sits idle |
| Failover time | Near-instant, already serving | Requires promotion/startup of the passive |
| Complexity | Higher — data consistency across active nodes | Simpler — one writer at a time |

Active-active buys speed and full utilization at the cost of harder consistency; active-passive is simpler and cheaper but pays for that simplicity with slower failover.

slides.subTitle: What RTO/RPO each realistically achieves
slides.markdown:
**RTO** (Recovery Time Objective) is how long you can be down; **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective) is how much recent data you can afford to lose. Multi-AZ failover is fast — AZs are connected by low-latency links, so RTO can be seconds to minutes and RPO near-zero with synchronous replication.

Multi-region failover is slower and lossier by nature: replication across regions is usually **asynchronous** (cross-region latency makes synchronous writes impractical), so RPO is realistically seconds to minutes of data, and RTO includes DNS propagation and often a manual decision to fail over at all.

| Tier | What's running standby | Rough RTO |
|---|---|---|
| Backup-restore | Nothing — just backups | Hours to days |
| Pilot light | Minimal core (e.g. DB replica) | Tens of minutes |
| Warm standby | Scaled-down full stack | Minutes |
| Multi-site | Full-scale active-active | Seconds |

Each tier up costs more to run continuously, in exchange for a faster recovery. Picking a tier is choosing a point on the cost-vs-RTO curve for a specific service, not a one-size-fits-all default.

slides.subTitle: How the system decides "this is down"
slides.markdown:
Failover is only as good as the **health check** deciding when to trigger it. A check that's too shallow (e.g. "does the process respond to a TCP ping") can pass while the service is actually failing every real request — a false negative that leaves traffic flowing to a dead instance.

Good health checks probe a real dependency path (e.g. "can this instance actually query the database") and require **multiple consecutive failures** before declaring down, avoiding a flapping failover triggered by one transient blip.

slides.subTitle: DNS failover's inherent lag
slides.markdown:
DNS failover — updating a record to point at a healthy region — is simple and widely used, but it's slower than people assume. **TTL and caching** mean resolvers and clients keep using the old IP for a while after you change the record, regardless of what TTL you set, because not every resolver honors it strictly.

The belief "we set TTL to 60s so failover takes 60s" is optimistic — real-world propagation and caching (ISP resolvers, client-side caching, stale connection pools) routinely add minutes on top. Plan DR timing around that reality, not the textbook TTL number.

**Graceful degradation** means shedding non-critical features to keep the core function alive, instead of an all-or-nothing failure. An e-commerce site whose recommendation service is down should still let people **check out** — recommendations quietly disappear rather than the whole page 500ing.

This requires designing dependencies as **optional** ahead of time: timeouts, fallbacks, and feature flags that can disable a non-essential path without a deploy, so a single failing dependency doesn't cascade into a full outage.

slides.subTitle: Designing failover for a payment service with a 5-minute RTO
slides.markdown:
A 5-minute RTO rules out DNS-only multi-region failover (propagation lag alone can eat that budget) and rules out backup-restore or pilot-light tiers (too slow to spin up). It points to **warm standby or active-active within multi-AZ**, with automated health-check-driven failover — no human decision in the loop, since a human paging and deciding can itself take minutes.

RPO for payments also needs to be near-zero (can't silently lose a transaction), which pushes toward **synchronous replication within a region** rather than async cross-region — accepting that a full region loss has a slower, separate recovery path with a looser RPO.

slides.subTitle: Failover modes that fail
slides.markdown:
Two real failure classes turn an HA design meant to save you into the incident itself. **Split-brain**: a network partition makes both sides of an active-passive pair believe they're the primary, so both start accepting writes independently — recovering means reconciling two diverging write histories, sometimes losing data on one side no matter which you keep. Real systems avoid this with a **quorum or fencing** mechanism, such as STONITH ("shoot the other node in the head"), which forcibly kills the old primary before promoting a new one, rather than trusting both sides to peacefully agree who's in charge.

**Untested cold standby**: a passive replica or DR site that's provisioned but never actually promoted in a drill accumulates silent rot — expired credentials, drifted configuration, an unapplied schema migration — invisibly, because nothing ever exercises the path that would expose it. When a real failure finally calls on it, the "working" standby fails to come up at all. The only real defense is a scheduled, deliberate failover drill to the standby — treating a DR plan that's never been tested as unproven, not as working.
